newsitem.title: CONGO: FEATURE-Mobutu's designer refugees seek new homes in exile.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Mobutu's designer refugees seek new homes in exile.

text.p: Wealthy refugees from ousted Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko's extended clan have begun to drift from their haunts in neighbouring Congo for exile further afield.

The designer refugees, who fled Laurent Kabila's rebel alliance, clutch cellular phones and bulging leather suitcases with designer labels -- a world away from the emaciated Rwandan Hutu refugees scattered across eastern Zaire.
But they are unwelcome guests in a country which, like it or not, has to come to terms with a new reality in their old home across the River Zaire.
"We do want these people to leave Congo as quickly as possible," one Congolese presidential aide told Reuters on Sunday, one day after Kabila's rebels marched into the Zairean capital Kinshasa.
Some have already left.

The former president's army officer son, Captain Kongolo Mobutu, and up to 100 other clan members left Brazzaville on Monday night on a specially chartered aircraft to join Mobutu in Togo -- first stop on his own flight into exile.

"Not all of them were able to go and some are still here at the airport, possibly when the plane returns from Lome it will take them as well," said one official at Congo's national airline Lina Congo.
Mobutu Kongolo was an officer in Zaire's once-feared Presidential Guard, the only unit of the ragged army to attempt any real resistance to the rebels.
CLAN'S PRESENCE A PROBLEM
The presence of so many members of the clan in Congo was an embarrassment to the government, which was close to Mobutu, but must now deal with Kabila.

"In the end it is a matter of not giving Kabila's men a pretext for destabilising Congo," said Brazzaville daily Le Temps, explaining the government's desire to get rid of the Zaireans as quickly as possible.

The clan was forced to find a chartered jet after the crew refused to fly the presidential Boeing 727, saying it belonged to the Zairean state and not to Mobutu himself. Airline officials would not say who had paid for the charter.
The jet, named after Mobutu's birthplace town Lisala, stood idle on the tarmac of Brazzaville airport.

Mobutu, who is fighting cancer, prolonged what was meant to be a stopover in Togo on health grounds after his flight from his jungle palace in Gbadolite northern Zaire left him "very weak", a source close to the government there said.
Morocco and then France, a long-time Mobutu friend, were his likely next destinations, the source added.
BLURRED LINE BETWEEN PUBLIC AND PRIVATE PROPERTY
The line between public and private property became blurred in Mobutu's Zaire, where a corrupt elite thrived in one of the world's poorest countries.

Institutionalised theft and neglect impoverished what could have been one of the world's richest countries, with vast mineral deposits and fertile soil. Most of the 40 million people survived on little more than dreams of rising above the poverty line.

"We must just get out of here as quickly as we can," said the downhearted daughter of one of Mobutu's generals in Brazzaville. She nonetheless maintained impeccable style with bulbous gold earrings and a well-cut mango-coloured dress.
"Only this morning I was insulted by a Zairean taxi driver who said he didn't want people like me in his car," she said.
She hoped that eventually the family would find its way to South Africa, where property had long since been bought for just such an occasion.
But Zaire's new rulers, who have renamed the country the Democratic Republic of Congo, may not want to let matters rest there.
A rebel spokesman in France said after Kinshasa fell that Mobutu and his clan would be pursued.

"With us, he will never be in peace. Wherever he goes, we will find him," Zamba Afri Kounyen told radio France-Info on Sunday. "We regard them as criminals who must be detained and taken to trial by a people's court," he said.
He threatened "bombings" if France let the deposed leader settle there but he later rowed back, saying he spoke in the heat of the moment.
Zairean rebel representatives are urging countries, including the United States, France and Belgium, to freeze Mobutu assets.
Austria said on Monday it had contacted leading banks to establish whether Mobutu had concealed investments there. Switzerland has already moved to do so.
